a meal of adobo with fried rice and fried egg

parole.significato: Diospyros pilosanthera; a tree in the Ebenaceae family.
bitter melon

parole.testo: From Tagalog ampaw. Compare Spanish hampáo, Cebuano ampaw, Ilocano ampaw, Central Bikol ampaw, Aklanon ampaw, Maranao ampaw.

parole.significato: paternal grandfather; paternal grandpa
parole.testo: From Tagalog angkong, from Hokkien 俺公 (án-kong, “paternal grandfather”).

parole.significato: The breadfruit tree.
Traditional Philippine stickfighting, a martial art.
parole.testo: From Tagalog arnis, from Spanish arnés in the archaic sense of “a chivalric set of weapons or armor” (compare English harness).

parole.significato: A variety of mongrel free-ranging dog found in the Philippines.
parole.testo: From Tagalog askal, a blend of aso (“dog”) + kalye (“street”).

parole.significato: Synonym of askal.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog aspin, a blend of aso + Pinoy, suggested by the Philippine Animal Welfare Society as an alternative to askal.

parole.significato: An elder sister
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog ate (“elder sister”), from Hokkien 阿姊 (á-ché, “eldest sister”).

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of San Francisco, Quezon.
A member of the Philippines national football team.
parole.testo: Stylized from Tagalog askal. The term came into use in 2005, months before the Southeast Asian Games in the Philippines.

parole.significato: A fish corral

Expressing the fatalistic attitude that things are out of one's control and whatever will happen will happen.
A Filipino returning to the Philippines after spending time in another country.
parole.testo: From Tagalog balikbayan, from balik (“to return”) + bayan (“home country”).

money, food, or other provisions taken to school, work, or on a journey.
leader of a barangay
parole.testo: From barangay + captain, with the former from Tagalog barangay.

parole.significato: gang; clique; informal group of friends
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog barkada, from Philippine Spanish barcada (“gang of friends”), from Spanish barcada (“shipload”).

parole.significato: A traditional Philippine costume comprising a blouse and long skirt.

A hovel or shanty.
Of, or pertaining to Batangas.
parole.testo: From Tagalog Batangueño, from Spanish batangueño, from Batangas + -eño.

Mutual cooperation for the public good.

parole.testo: From Tagalog bibingka, from Malay bingka (“cake made of rice flour, coconut milk, eggs and palm sugar”), as in Malay kuih bingka. See also Indonesian kue bingka, Macanese bebinca.

parole.significato: A tree from the Philippines, which bears small, edible fruit in clusters, Antidesma bunius.
A sautéed pork dish of the Philippines, flavoured with shrimp paste.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog binagoongan (literally “that to which bagoong (shrimp paste) is applied”).

parole.significato: A Filipino dish consisting of thinly-sliced beefsteak braised in soy sauce, calamansi juice, garlic, ground black peppe…
parole.testo: From Tagalog bistek, from Spanish bistec, from English beefsteak. Doublet of beefsteak and bifshtek.

parole.significato: Synonym of bistek.
a meal of beefsteak with fried rice and fried egg
A brushy, rural area or location.

parole.significato: Jian dui; sesame ball.
parole.testo: From Tagalog butsi / butse, possibly from Hokkien 麻糍 (môa-chî) or a similar cognate, or Spanish buche (“gulp a mouthful”). Compare Cebuano butsi (“Jian dui”), Tagalog matse (“Mache”), Cebuano masi (“Masi”), Kapampangan motsi (“Moche”).

parole.significato: A coconut.
The youngest child in a family.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog bunso, from earlier bungso, an early borrowing from Malay bongsu (“lastborn”), ultimately from Proto-Malayo-Polynesian *buŋsu.

parole.significato: A fibre obtained from palms of the genus Corypha.
Land that has been cleared using slash-and-burn techniques.
frangipani; plumeria
Synonym of calamondin.
Of, or pertaining to Cavite.
parole.testo: From Tagalog Caviteño, from Spanish caviteño, from Cavite + -eño.

parole.significato: A Chinese Filipino (a Filipino with Chinese descent, whether mixed or pure ethnic Chinese, especially one who identifie…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog Tsinoy, modeled after a blend of Spanish chino (“Chinese”) + Tagalog Pinoy (“Filipino”). See also Indonesian chindo.

parole.significato: Dried fish, usually split open (though they may be left whole), gutted, salted liberally, and then sun- and air-dried.
Milkfish daing.
A young woman who has passed puberty but is not yet married; an eligible young woman.
parole.testo: From Tagalog dalaga (“maiden; virgin; unmarried girl”).

parole.significato: Dracontomelon dao; a large tree of the family Anacardiaceae; the argus pheasant tree.
The Indian coral tree, Erythrina variegata.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog or Cebuano, from Proto-Malayo-Polynesian *dapdap.

parole.significato: A member or supporter of the Liberal Party of the Philippines or the Aquino political dynasty.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog dilawan, from dilaw (“yellow”).

parole.significato: A savoury Filipino stew of meat and/or offal simmered in a gravy of pig blood, garlic, chili and vinegar.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog duwende, from Spanish duende (“goblin, elf”). Doublet of duende.

parole.significato: Synonym of ensaimada.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog ensaymada, from Spanish ensaimada, from Catalan ensaïmada. Doublet of ensaimada.

parole.significato: The traditional martial arts of the Philippines, which emphasize the use of sticks, knives, and various improvised weap…
parole.testo: From Tagalog escrima or eskrima, borrowed from Spanish esgrima, noun form of the verb esgrimir (“to handle a melee weapon whether for offensive or defensive purposes”).

parole.significato: Colocasia esculenta, raised as a food primarily for its corm, which distantly resembles potato.
Inducing an intense emotion by being cute or charming; grittingly thrilling
A Filipino person.
parole.testo: First attested circa 1899, in US military slang, probably from American soldiers during the Philippine-American War hearing Tagalog gago (“idiot; fool; simpleton”) and Tagalog gaga (“female idiot; female fool”) and considering it to sound like babbling (goo goo ga ga). Possibly influenced by goo-goo

parole.significato: Gelatin made from agar, used in certain foods.

parole.testo: From Tagalog halo-halo, a reduplication of halo (“mix”).

parole.significato: A traditional healing practice, involving chiropractic manipulation and massage.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog hopia, from Spanish hopia, from Hokkien, possibly 好餅 /好饼 (hó piáⁿ, literally “good pastry”) according to Chan-Yap (1980) and Manuel (1948). See also Early Manila Hokkien 香餅 /香饼 (hioⁿ-piáⁿ, literally “fragrant pastry”), Indonesian bakpia. Compare Cebuano hopya.

parole.significato: A member of the Hukbalahap.
parole.testo: Clipping of Hukbalahap, from Tagalog Hukbalahap, an abbreviation of Hukbong Bayan Laban sa Hapon (“People's Army Against the Japanese”). The initial word itself where the abbreviation comes from is from Tagalog hukbo (“army”), which itself is derived from Hokkien 服務 /服务 (ho̍k-bū, “service”).

parole.significato: A member of this movement.
A member of any of several Austronesian ethnic groups in the Philippines, inhabiting the mountains of Luzon.
A native or inhabitant of Iloilo.
parole.testo: From Tagalog Ilonggo, from Spanish ilongo, from ilong + -o, the root referring to Hiligaynon ilong (“nose”), from the nose-like shape of the land between the Iloilo River and Batiano River where the Spanish Fort San Pedro is located. See also Spanish pampango.

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of Infanta, Quezon.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog Infantahin, from Infanta + -hin.

parole.significato: A supporter of 14th Philippine vice-president Leni Robredo on her 2022 Philippine presidential election campaign.
Any of various dessert rice cakes.
A goat stew from the Philippines, commonly made with vegetables and liver paste.
parole.testo: From Tagalog kaldereta, from Spanish caldereta, from caldero + -eta.

parole.significato: A Filipino sword akin to the kris.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog kalis, from Malay keris, from Old Javanese kĕris, kris Doublet of kris.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog Kano, initial clipping of Amerikano, ultimately from Spanish americano (“male American”).

parole.significato: An office boy.
parole.testo: Originally from Japanese 官庁 (kanchō, “government office”) + boy, borrowed in during WW2 according to Potet (2016), but the former eventually got replaced with Tagalog kanto (“corner, especially of two streets”).

parole.significato: A Philippine stew of peanuts with meat (often oxtail), seafood, and/or vegetables.
frying pan
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog kawali, from Malay kuali, from Tamil குவளை (kuvaḷai, “wide-mouthed vessel; cup”).

parole.significato: A glutinous rice dish of the Philippines, with meat, vegetables, etc.
parole.testo: From Tagalog kiyampong, from Hokkien 鹹飯 /咸饭 (kiâm-pn̄g).

parole.significato: A flirtatious girl or woman.

parole.significato: excited; thrilled; the feeling of butterflies in one's stomach due to romantic tension.
shared or split cost (usually for meals together with people, where each one pays their own cost)
parole.testo: From Tagalog KKB, initialism of kani-kaniyang bayad (“going Dutch”, adjective, literally “to each their own payment”).

parole.significato: prawn crackers
parole.testo: From Tagalog kropek. Compare Malay keropok, Indonesian kerupuk, Dutch kroepoek.

parole.significato: a boat-shaped lute
parole.testo: From Tagalog kudyapi, Hiligaynon kudyapi and Cebuano kudyapi.

parole.significato: An elder brother.
parole.testo: From Tagalog kuya, from Hokkien 哥仔 (*ko-iá).

parole.significato: A tree with flavorful and nutritious leaves, the moringa or horseradish tree, Moringa oleifera.

parole.testo: From Tagalog nido (“edible bird's nest”) + soup. Tagalog nido itself is from Spanish nido (“nest”). See also El Nido in Palawan, where the edible bird's nest is historically harvested from by a Busyador.

parole.significato: A godmother.

parole.testo: From Tagalog, a reversed form of pinoy.

parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog pabebe + wave. First attested in 2015.

parole.significato: paddy
parole.testo: From Tagalog palay. Doublet of paddy.

parole.significato: A small, flat, sweet rice cake eaten in the Philippines.
A low-income male homosexual who behaves in a feminine manner and stereotypically works in a beauty parlor.
An ornamental star-like Christmas lantern from the Philippines.
parole.testo: From Tagalog parol, from Spanish farol (“lantern”).

parole.significato: A gift brought back by a traveller for somebody at home.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog pasalubong, literally "(something) for when you welcome me".

parole.significato: A tropical tree, Canarium ovatum, native to maritime Southeast Asia, New Guinea and northern Australia, and cultivated…

A Filipino; a citizen or local inhabitant of the Philippines and those descending from such, especially a male.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog Pinoy. Pinoy caught on with the Florante song “Ako'y isang Pinoy” ("I am a Pinoy"), which became popular in Filipino culture to denote their country of origin and background. parole.significato: finger food
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog pulutan, from pulot + -an.

parole.testo: Calque of Tagalog itlog na pula.

parole.significato: A roundabout; traffic circle.

parole.significato: A convenience store in the Philippines; a neighborhood variety store; a minimarket selling basic necessities.
parole.testo: From Tagalog sari-sari + store. Tagalog sari-sari is a reduplication of sari.

parole.significato: A skirt.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog saya, from Spanish saya.

parole.significato: a favored customer; a regular who receives preferential treatment
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog suki, from Hokkien 主客 (chú-kheh, “regular customer or dealer”, literally “principal guest”).

parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog taho, from Hokkien 豆腐 (tāu-hū, “tofu”) or perhaps 豆腐花 (tāu-hū-hoe, “tofu pudding”) that it might simply be short for.

parole.significato: Cake of salted fermented bean curd.
A small, dark brown, hoofed buffalo, Bubalus mindorensis, found only in Mindoro in the Philippines.
An idler; a layabout.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog tambay, itself from English stand by.

parole.significato: A low-level law enforcement officer.
Seasoned slices of dried or cured meat in Filipino cuisine.
A meal of tapa with fried rice and fried egg.
Salted black beans.
parole.testo: From Tagalog tausi, from Hokkien 豆豉 (tāu-sī). Doublet of douchi.

parole.significato: A native or inhabitant of Tayabas, Quezon.
A native or inhabitant of Tayabas, Quezon.
parole.testo: From Tagalog Tayabense, from Spanish tayabense, from Tayabas + -ense.

parole.significato: A person from Quezon and Aurora provinces.
parole.testo: From Tagalog Tayabeño, from Spanish tayabeño, from Tayabas + -eño.

parole.significato: A Philippine television drama, serialized in the manner of a soap opera.

An aunt; auntie.
parole.testo: From Tagalog tita, from Spanish tita.

parole.significato: An uncle.
parole.testo: From Tagalog tito, from Spanish tito.

parole.significato: A Philippine omelette of ground meat and potatoes.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog torta, from Spanish torta, from Latin turta, thought to derive from Latin tŏrta f (“twisted”). Doublet of torte and tart.

parole.significato: a meal of tocino with fried rice and fried egg
soy sauce
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog toyo, from Hokkien 豆油 (tāu-iû, “soy sauce”).

parole.significato: soy sauce mixed with calamansi juice
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog toyomansi, a blend of toyo + kalamansi.

parole.significato: corrupt politician
parole.testo: Contraction of traditional politician; also influenced by Tagalog trapo (“rag”), from Spanish trapo.

parole.significato: yangmei
parole.testo: From Tagalog tsampoy, from Cantonese 陳皮梅 /陈皮梅 (can⁴ pei⁴ mui⁴⁻²), introduced as a genericized trademark romanized as "CHAN PUI MUI" as printed on preserved prune packaging.

parole.significato: A reddish palm wine made from coconut or nipa sap.
A Philippine snack made of a fried and caramelized spring roll wrapping thinly sliced bananas.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Tagalog turon, from Spanish turrón.

parole.significato: The purple yam, Dioscorea alata.
An illegal betting game using an arcade machine playing horse racing.
parole.testo: video + Tagalog karera (“race”), from the horse racing games played in the machines.

parole.significato: A nanny; female caregiver; nursemaid
parole.testo: From Tagalog yaya, from Philippine Spanish yaya.

parole.significato: The fragrant flower of a tropical tree (Cananga odorata) native to southeast Asia.
parole.testo: Via Early Modern Spanish, from Tagalog ilang-ilang, from either ilang (“wilderness”) or ilang-ilan (“rare”).
